bib.title: Bandit Algorithms, Chapter 7: The Upper Confidence Bound Algorithm

question: How can the optimism principle give a bandit algorithm (UCB) with finite-time regret guarantees comparable to explore-then-commit without knowing the suboptimality gaps?
hypothesis: UCB matches ETC's regret guarantees without prior knowledge of the gaps, and behaves well with more than two arms.

limits: delta = 1/n^2 needs the horizon n in advance; a smaller delta improves regret and empirical performance, and a t-dependent delta removes the dependence (Ch. 8) (Notes 1).
Instance bound is meaningless if a single suboptimal gap is tiny; Thm 7.2 addresses that.
Analysis assumes 1-subgaussian noise with known constant; unknown variance, heavy tails left to exercises 7.2, 7.6, 7.7.
Optimism is not universal: fails when an action gives no feedback about itself or gives feedback about other actions (linear bandits, Ch. 25).
Experiment 7.1 is brief (2 arms, n=1000, Gaussian); number of simulation runs, seeds and the delta used for UCB are not stated in this chapter.
practices: Choose delta about 1/n^2 for the proof (a bit smaller than 1/n because T_i(t-1) is random) (p.105-108).
Index = empirical mean + exploration bonus sqrt(2 log(1/delta)/T_i(t-1)); pull each arm once first via infinite index when T_i = 0 (Eq 7.2).
Compare algorithms empirically as well as by theory, and prove lower bounds (p.109).
For rewards in [0,1] (1/2-subgaussian) adjust the width (Exercise 7.2); for unknown variance with bounded noise use empirical Bernstein (Ex. 7.6).

code.snippet: Input k and delta; for t in 1..n: A_t = argmax_i UCB_i(t-1, delta); observe X_t, update. UCB_i(t-1,delta) = inf if T_i(t-1)=0 else mu_hat_i(t-1) + sqrt(2 log(1/delta) / T_i(t-1))
